metaDescription: Walk-behind leaf blowers compared on engine, impeller, CFM and MPH, wheels and control, with picks for big lawns, driveways and light commercial work.
expertTake: The Billy Goat F902H with a Honda GX270 is the best walk-behind blower here for pros and large properties, the Champion 212cc is the sensible pick for homeowners with an acre or more, and the YARDMAX YF1565 is the value pick. Skip a walk-behind if your yard is small or full of tight beds: a handheld or backpack is far easier to steer.
introParagraphs: A walk-behind blower is a small engine and a big fan on wheels. Instead of carrying a nozzle, you steer a machine that pushes a wide, powerful column of air ahead of it, which clears leaves, grass clippings and debris from open ground far faster than a handheld can. It is closer to a lawn tool than a hand tool.

Because the machine rolls, weight is not the limit. The factors that matter are engine size, fan design, wheel quality and how well the discharge can be aimed. This guide compares those in six walk-behind models and explains why the headline airflow numbers need cautious reading.

products.name: Billy Goat F902H Honda GX270 Commercial

specList.label: Control
specList.value: Fingertip lever directs airflow up or down

products.description:
Billy Goat is a long-standing commercial blower maker, and the F902H pairs a Honda GX270 with a rounded housing designed to reduce noise by removing air voids. A fingertip lever aims the airflow up or down, which is a practical advantage when you move between flat lawn and heaped debris.

Large pneumatic rear wheels reduce rolling resistance on rough terrain, and thicker padded handles lower vibration and fatigue. A Honda GX270 is the common commercial engine and is well supported.

This is a professional machine at a professional price tier. It is more than a homeowner needs, but for landscapers, schools and campuses it earns its keep. Standard oil and filter service apply. Because it is built for daily service, a dealer can supply belts, wheels and gaskets years from now. Budget for a trailer ramp, since it is not a machine you lift by hand. Its rounded housing is also easier to clean after wet leaf jobs.
products.bestFor: Landscapers and large properties that run a blower for hours each week.
pros: Honda GX270 engine with wide service support
Fingertip control aims airflow up or down
Pneumatic wheels roll over rough ground
cons: Heavy to load into a truck

products.name: Champion 212cc 1200 CFM Walk-Behind
products.description:
Champion builds this around a 212cc engine, an adjustable throttle and 12-inch never-flat rear wheels. A solid wheel cannot puncture on a stick or thorn, which solves the most common tire complaint on yard equipment. The front wheel locks for straight runs or swivels 360 degrees for turns.

The adjustable throttle lets you reduce power near beds and plants. The handle height adjusts, which is a real comfort feature for tall or short users.

Compared with the Billy Goat, it has a generic engine and a lower price tier, though Champion has a larger service network than most importers. Expect the usual upkeep of oil, plug and fuel care. Keep the throttle low when you work near beds, then open it up in the open lawn. Check the handle height each time a different person uses it. Because it has no tires to inflate, storage is easier.
products.bestFor: Homeowners with one to three acres of open lawn.
cons: Heavy to store without a ramp
Less airflow control than the Billy Goat

products.name: YARDMAX YF1565 209cc Walk-Behind
products.description:
YARDMAX offers a 209cc overhead-valve engine with 150 MPH and 1200 CFM listed as maximums, a spec sheet that matches the Champion's on paper. The listing is sparse, but the core hardware is the same recipe as the rest of the class.

The point of buying it is price, as it sits at a lower tier than the Champion and Billy Goat. In return you get less documentation and a thinner support network.

For an acre or two of open lawn it moves a lot of leaves quickly. Maintain it like any four-stroke engine, with oil changes and fresh fuel. Because the listing is sparse, confirm the return policy and parts availability before buying. Check all fasteners after the first hour of use, as vibration loosens bolts on budget machines. It makes sense mainly for seasonal use.
products.bestFor: Budget buyers with open lawns who want walk-behind capacity.

products.name: Landworks 7HP 212cc Jet Sweep Walk-Behind
products.description:
Landworks calls this a Jet Sweep blower, a term for walk-behind units with a large impeller housing that directs a wide stream of air ahead of the wheels. A 7 horsepower, 212cc OHV engine drives it, with manual propulsion.

The design is aimed at garden and lawn applications, with enough power to move leaves, grass clippings and light debris across a large area. The listing focuses on safety, so follow the manual and keep bystanders away.

It competes with the YARDMAX on paper and sits near it on price. Parts are generic, so basic upkeep is simple. Read the safety section before first use, since a machine this size can throw debris far. Wear eye and hearing protection and keep bystanders and pets away. Rinse out debris from the housing after use.
products.bestFor: Large lawns and gardens with leaves and light debris.
pros: Jet Sweep housing moves wide stream

products.name: SuperHandy 7HP 209cc 1270 CFM Walk-Behind
products.description:
SuperHandy documents its machine well: a 7 horsepower, 209cc four-stroke engine, 150 MPH, 1270 CFM and a 14.2-inch plastic impeller on a powder-coated steel frame. A plastic impeller reduces weight and cost, and for leaf and grass clippings it is adequate, though hard debris like stones can chip it.

Two large 12-inch rear wheels and an 8-inch swivel front wheel handle most lawns. The maker specifies unleaded 87-octane fuel, with 10 percent ethanol or less recommended.

It competes with the Champion on airflow. The tradeoff is service coverage and the plastic impeller. If you blow gravel edges, clear loose stones first to protect the plastic impeller. Store it under cover, because the frame coating is good but the engine hates moisture. Check the impeller for chips each season.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a well-documented mid-priced walk-behind.
cons: Plastic impeller can chip on stones

products.name: SuperHandy Jet Sweep 7HP 212cc 2000 CFM 200 MPH
products.description:
This SuperHandy model claims 2000 CFM and 200 MPH from a 7 horsepower, 212cc engine at 3600 rpm, far above the 1200 to 1270 CFM claims of similar-engine rivals. A larger engine is not behind that gap; the difference is more likely in how the figures are measured.

Treat the numbers as marketing ceilings. The same 7 HP class engine drives the Champion at 1200 CFM, and an engine cannot produce twice the air from the same power without a different test method.

The machine is a capable Jet Sweep style blower. Buy it for the build and price, not for the 2000 CFM. Compare it with the Landworks on engine and price, since the hardware is nearly identical. Run the first tank gently and check the oil level before every session. Do not buy it on the 2000 CFM number alone.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a Jet Sweep style blower and accept inflated claims.
cons: 2000 CFM claim is not credible next to rivals

buyingCriteria.explanation: A Honda GX270, as on the Billy Goat F902H, is a commercial engine with wide service support. Generic 209 to 212cc engines on the Champion, YARDMAX, Landworks and SuperHandy deliver similar power on paper but have thinner service coverage. If the machine earns money, pay for the engine. Ask whether you will still be using the machine in ten years; if yes, an engine with parts support is cheap insurance.

buyingCriteria.criterion: How to read the CFM claims
buyingCriteria.explanation: The Champion and YARDMAX list 1200 CFM, the SuperHandy lists 1270 and the Jet Sweep SuperHandy claims 2000 from the same 7 HP class engine. Real airflow cannot double from the same power, so treat claims as unreliable across brands. A fair comparison is to look at engine horsepower first, then treat airflow as an unproven extra. If a seller will not give the engine model number, assume a generic engine.

A plastic impeller, as on the SuperHandy 14.2-inch, is light and cheap but can chip if it ingests stones. Metal impellers resist damage better. If you blow gravel drives, choose accordingly. Pick up a handful of gravel and ask whether your drive sheds stones into the lawn; if so, favor a stronger impeller.

Never-flat 12-inch wheels, as on the Champion, eliminate punctures. A locking, swiveling front wheel helps both straight runs and turns. Large pneumatic wheels, as on the Billy Goat, roll better over rough ground. Roll the machine across your own lawn mentally: soft ground and ruts punish small wheels.

The Billy Goat's fingertip lever aims airflow up or down, and the Champion has an adjustable throttle. Fixed-output machines blow mulch out of beds. Control matters on mixed terrain. Aiming the air downward helps with wet leaves and aiming it up helps with deep piles on a driveway.

These machines weigh as much as a push mower and have a long handle. Measure your garage and ramp before buying. Fold-down handles help, though not all models have them. Many of these have no folding handle, so measure the garage door and the truck bed before you order.

specDecoder.meaning: Air volume per minute at the nozzle. It is maker-measured, so compare within a class. Think of it as a rough ranking tool only.
specDecoder.watchFor: 1200 CFM on the Champion versus a claimed 2000 CFM on the Jet Sweep SuperHandy.

specDecoder.meaning: Air speed at the nozzle. Higher speed lifts wet debris. A faster stream lifts wet leaves but scatters mulch.
specDecoder.watchFor: 150 MPH on most, 200 MPH claimed on the Jet Sweep.

specDecoder.meaning: An overhead valve engine that runs on straight gasoline. It avoids fuel mixing. No fuel and oil mixing, which simplifies ownership.
specDecoder.watchFor: All the units here use it.

specDecoder.meaning: Solid wheels that cannot puncture. They avoid flats from sticks and thorns. They also keep rolling after a long storage, with no pump or valve to fail.
A design with a wide impeller housing for a wide airstream. It is the common walk-behind layout.
specDecoder.watchFor: Landworks and SuperHandy use the term.

howWeEvaluated.title: Engine and support
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the Honda GX270 on the Billy Goat with generic 209 to 212cc engines. Service coverage earned the biggest bonus. Commercial engine support was weighted heavily because downtime is the real cost in service.

howWeEvaluated.title: Airflow credibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We treated claimed CFM as marketing and penalized claims that exceeded what a 7 HP engine plausibly produces. The 2000 CFM claim scored poorly. We applied a plausibility check to every airflow claim, comparing it to engine horsepower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Chassis and wheels
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at wheel size, puncture resistance and frame coating. The Champion and Billy Goat earned the most credit. Never-flat wheels and large pneumatic tires were compared on rolling resistance and puncture risk.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed throttle control and airflow aiming, noting the Billy Goat's fingertip lever. Handles and controls were compared for vibration comfort over a long session.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated the YARDMAX as the value pick from the Billy Goat as the professional pick. Owner feedback patterns on generic imports shaped the scoring. We also noted listing completeness, since sparse listings make verification harder.

cards.label: Generic
cards.text: The Champion, YARDMAX, Landworks and SuperHandy models use 209 to 212cc engines with similar output and thin service coverage.

cards.label: Commercial
cards.text: The Billy Goat F902H uses a Honda GX270 with wide service support and a refined housing.

howToChoose.note: Pick generic if you blow occasionally, commercial if the machine pays for itself.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a wide stream, an engine with torque and wheels that roll easily. Work with the wind and push leaves into a line.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Billy Goat F902H and Champion 212cc are the most controllable, and the Jet Sweep models give a wide stream.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you blow weekly over several acres or for pay, which points to the Billy Goat F902H.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you only blow in autumn. The YARDMAX or Landworks handle seasonal use at a lower price.

maintenance.why: Engines run hard in dusty work. Fresh oil protects bearings.
Dust clogs filters fast and starves the engine.
Chips or cracks cause vibration. Replace damaged impellers.
Pneumatic tires on the Billy Goat need even pressure.
Old ethanol fuel gums the carburetor.

faq.a: Walk-behind for open lawns of one acre or more, where you can push a machine. Backpack for tight areas, steps and beds.

No. Similar 7 HP engines claim anywhere from 1200 to 2000 CFM. Use engine class and brand as your guide. Ask the seller for the engine model and check that the horsepower is realistic for the claimed airflow before you pay.

faq.q: Do walk-behind blowers need mixed fuel?
faq.a: No. These use four-stroke engines on straight unleaded gasoline.
They move wet leaves better than most handhelds thanks to volume, but speed matters too, so go slower.
Yes, they are as loud as any gas engine. Wear hearing protection. Hearing damage is cumulative, so use earmuffs or plugs on every session even for short jobs.
Many seasons with oil changes and fuel care. Commercial engines last longest.
